title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
subtitle: Separating what a system does from the operational constraints and quality attributes under which it must perform.
keyTakeaways: Functional requirements define user-visible features and API behaviors, while non-functional requirements (NFRs) dictate architecture.
Two systems with identical functional requirements (e.g., 'post a message') require radically different architectures when NFRs shift from 100 DAU to 500M DAU.
Always quantify NFRs during the first 5 minutes of a system design interview using concrete metrics (p99 latency, availability nines, RPO/RTO).

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: In a small CRUD application, functional requirements dominate engineering effort. At scale, non-functional requirements (NFRs), also known as quality attributes or '-ilities', are the primary drivers of architectural complexity. Anyone can build a timeline query using a SQL JOIN for 1,000 users; doing it for 300 million daily active users with sub-200ms p99 latency forces you to introduce fan-out-on-write caches, celebrity hybrid fan-out, and read-optimized stores.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Functional requirements define user-visible features and API behaviors, while non-functional requirements (NFRs) dictate architecture.
**Problem Space & Invariants**: Two systems with identical functional requirements (e.g., 'post a message') require radically different architectures when NFRs shift from 100 DAU to 500M DAU.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements:
bullets: **Strict NFRs (99.999% SLA, Strong Consistency)**: Provides zero data anomalies, simple mental model for application developers, enterprise-grade trust. Best suited for Financial ledgers, billing systems, inventory reservation, and authentication services.

**Relaxed NFRs (99.9% SLA, Eventual Consistency)**: Provides ultra-fast local reads/writes, resilient to network partitions, dramatically lower cloud spend. Best suited for Social media feeds, view counters, product recommendations, and activity streams.
Functional Requirements: Deterministic business rules, API endpoints, state transitions, and user workflows.
Non-Functional Requirements: Scalability, availability, latency targets, consistency guarantees, durability, security, and cost ceilings.
Read-heavy (100:1 read/write) + Eventual Consistency -> Multi-tier caching (CDN + Redis) and read replicas.
Strict zero-data-loss (RPO = 0) + Strong Consistency -> Quorum or synchronous replication with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and fsync.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Financial ledgers, billing systems, inventory reservation, and authentication services, suited for environments requiring Zero data anomalies, simple mental model for application developers, enterprise-grade trust.

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Social media feeds, view counters, product recommendations, and activity streams, where Ultra-fast local reads/writes, resilient to network partitions, dramatically lower cloud spend.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: Every NFR statement maps directly to a set of infrastructure patterns. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: high write latency across regions, 3x-5x infrastructure cost, complex consensus protocols (raft/paxos).
**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: users may briefly see stale data, requires conflict resolution (lww or crdts) in the app layer.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Always quantify NFRs during the first 5 minutes of a system design interview using concrete metrics (p99 latency, availability nines, RPO/RTO).

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Never ask the interviewer 'What are the non-functional requirements?' Instead, propose sensible defaults based on the domain: 'Since this is a social feed, I suggest optimizing for high availability and sub-200ms p99 read latency with eventual consistency, rather than strong consistency. Does that align with your expectations?'
